period.label: About AD 65-80
period.note: This follows the traditional date. The letter gives no date or place; scholars' dates range from the 50s to the early second century.

rulers.name: Nero, then Vespasian and Titus
rulers.text: Nero's death in AD 68 was followed by civil war. Vespasian, the general fighting in Judea, won the throne in AD 69, and his son Titus finished the war and later succeeded him.

rulers.name: Herod Agrippa II
rulers.text: Ruled territories north and east of Galilee under Rome. He tried to talk Jerusalem out of revolt in AD 66 and stayed on Rome's side.

rulers.name: Roman governors of Judea
rulers.text: Judea was ruled by Roman governors until the revolt. After AD 70 it became a separate province with a Roman legion stationed in ruined Jerusalem.

events.title: James, Jude's brother, is killed
events.text: The high priest Ananus had "James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ" stoned in Jerusalem. Jude names himself "brother of James."

events.title: Nero blames the Christians for Rome's fire
events.text: After the Great Fire of Rome, Nero put a "vast multitude" of Christians to death.

events.title: The Jewish revolt begins
events.text: Jerusalem rose against Rome after the governor Florus seized money from the temple treasury.

events.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
events.text: After Nero's suicide, Galba, Otho and Vitellius each seized power and fell within months, until Vespasian won.

events.title: Jerusalem and its temple destroyed
events.text: Titus took Jerusalem after a five-month siege and the temple was burned, as Jesus had foretold.

events.title: The fall of Masada
events.text: The last rebels held out on the desert fortress of Masada above the Dead Sea until a Roman siege ramp reached its walls.

events.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
events.text: The eruption of Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in Italy.

events.title: The Colosseum opens
events.text: Titus opened the great amphitheater in Rome, built partly with spoils from the Jewish war.

events.title: Jude's grandsons before Domitian
events.text: An early church historian records that Domitian summoned two grandsons of Jude, "the brother of the Lord," as descendants of David. Finding them poor farmers with hard hands, he let them go.

places.name: Sodom and Gomorrha
places.summary: Named by Jude as an example of judgment. Cities of the plain near the Dead Sea, destroyed in Abraham's day.

facts.text: The LORD rained fire and brimstone on Sodom and Gomorrha after the men of Sodom tried to seize the two angels staying with Lot.
The prophets, Jesus and Peter all point back to Sodom and Gomorrha as a warning of judgment.
Genesis places them in the plain of Jordan near the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea). Their exact sites have never been agreed.

life.text: The Gospels name Jesus' brothers as James, Joses, Simon and Judas (Jude). They did not believe in him during his ministry, but after the resurrection they were with the disciples praying.

life.topic: Michael and the body of Moses
life.text: Deuteronomy says no one knows where Moses was buried. The story of Michael disputing with the devil over his body is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers say it came from a Jewish book called the Assumption of Moses. Michael appears in Scripture as a chief angel.

Genesis records Enoch, seventh from Adam, who "walked with God." The words Jude quotes match a passage of 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read at the time; Aramaic fragments of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
sources: Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4 (Enoch fragments)

life.text: Each name points to an Old Testament story: Cain killed his brother, Balaam was hired to curse Israel, and Korah (Core) led a rebellion against Moses.
Early Christians shared common meals when they met, along with the Lord's Supper. Paul rebukes the Corinthians for selfishness at these meals.
The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, yet that generation died in the wilderness because they did not believe.

basis: Scripture first, then ancient writers on these years (Josephus, Tacitus, Suetonius, Eusebius) and on the Jewish writings Jude draws on. Drafted by Claude and not yet reviewed by a person.
